# On the power of adaptivity in statistical adversaries

**Authors:** Guy Blanc Stanford Jane Lange MIT Ali Malik Stanford Li-Yang Tan Stanford

## Abstract

We study a fundamental question concerning adversarial noise models in statistical problems where the algorithm receives i.i.d. draws from a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . The definitions of these adversaries specify the type of allowable corruptions (noise model) as well as when these corruptions can be made (adaptivity); the latter differentiates between oblivious adversaries that can only corrupt the distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and adaptive adversaries that can have their corruptions depend on the specific sample $S$ that is drawn from $\mathcal{D}$ .

In this work, we investigate whether oblivious adversaries are effectively equivalent to adaptive adversaries, across all noise models studied in the literature. Specifically, can the behavior of an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of oblivious adversaries always be well-approximated by that of an algorithm $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ in the presence of adaptive adversaries? Our first result shows that this is indeed the case for the broad class of statistical query algorithms, under all reasonable noise models. We then show that in the specific case of additive noise, this equivalence holds for all algorithms. Finally, we map out an approach towards proving this statement in its fullest generality, for all algorithms and under all reasonable noise models.

## 1 Introduction

The possibility of noise pervades most problems in statistical estimation and learning. In this paper we will be concerned with adversarial noise models, as opposed to the class of more benign random noise models. Adversarial noise models are the subject of intensive study across statistics [Hub64, Ham71, Tuk75], learning theory [Val85, Hau92, KL93, KSS94, BEK02], and algorithms [DKK+19, LRV16, CSV17, DK19]. The definition of each model specifies:

- 1. The type of corruptions allowed. For example, the adversary may be allowed to add arbitrary points (additive noise [Hub64, Val85]), or in the context of supervised learning, allowed to change the labels in the data (agnostic noise [Hau92, KSS94]).

- 2. The adaptivity of the adversary.

The latter is the focus of our work. Consider any statistical problem where the algorithm is given i.i.d. draws from a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . On one hand we have oblivious adversaries: such an adversary corrupts $\mathcal{D}$ to a different distribution $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ , from which the algorithm then receives a sample. On the other hand we have adaptive adversaries: such an adversary first draws a sample $\bm{S}$ from $\mathcal{D}$ , and upon seeing the specific outcomes in $\bm{S}$ , corrupts it to $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ which is then passed on to the algorithm. One can further consider adversaries with intermediate adaptive power, but we think of this as a dichotomy for now. A coupling argument shows that adaptive adversaries are at least as powerful as oblivious ones [DKK+19, ZJS19]. In this work we investigate whether they can be strictly more powerful.

#### Question 1.

Fix the type of corruptions allowed. Is it true that for any algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ , there is an algorithm $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ whose behavior in the presence of adaptive adversaries well-approximates that of $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of oblivious adversaries?

The distinction between oblivious and adaptive adversaries is frequently touched upon in works concerning statistical problems. Sometimes this distinction is brought up in service of emphasizing that the algorithms given in these works are robust against adaptive adversaries; other times it is brought up when the algorithms are shown to be robust against oblivious adversaries, and the viewpoint of an adaptive corruption process is provided as intuition for the noise model. However, the relative power of oblivious and adaptive adversaries in the statistical setting has not been systematically considered in the literature.

### 1.1 Our contributions

#### 1.1.1 A unified framework for characterizing data adversaries.

To reason generally about Question 1, we associate every type of allowable corruptions with a cost function $\rho$ between distributions. An oblivious $\rho$ -adversary therefore corrupts $\mathcal{D}$ to some $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ that is $\eta$ -close with respect to $\rho$ , meaning that $\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\leq\eta$ . An adaptive $\rho$ -adversary corrupts a sample $S$ drawn from $\mathcal{D}$ to some $\widehat{S}$ such that the uniform distribution over $\widehat{S}$ is $\eta$ -close with respect to $\rho$ to that over $S$ .For example, when $\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})$ is the total variation distance between $\mathcal{D}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ , the resulting adaptive adversary represents nasty noise as defined in [BEK02], where the adversary is allowed to change an arbitrary $\eta$ -fraction of the points in $S$ . We discuss this framework in more detail in Section 3.

#### 1.1.2 Yes to Question 1 for all SQ algorithms

Our first result is an affirmative answer to Question 1 for the broad class of statistical query (SQ) algorithms. Our proof will require a mild assumption on this cost function, the precise statement of which we defer to the body of the paper. For now, we simply refer to cost functions satisfying this assumption as “reasonable”, and mention that it is easily satisfied by all standard noise models, and can be seen to be necessary for our result to hold.

#### Theorem 1 (SQ algorithms are robust to adaptive adversaries).

For all reasonable cost functions $\rho$ and SQ algorithms $\mathcal{A}$ , the behavior of $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of adaptive $\rho$ -adversaries well-approximates that of $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of oblivious adversaries.

A key ingredient in our proof of Footnote 1 is a novel reduction, using duality, from a $k$ -query SQ algorithm to a single “representative” SQ.

In other words, the SQ framework neutralizes adaptive adversaries into oblivious ones, and in the context of Question 1, we can take $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ to be $\mathcal{A}$ itself. Looking ahead to our other results, we remark that such a statement cannot be true for all algorithms: there are trivial examples of (non-SQ) algorithms $\mathcal{A}$ for which $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ has to be a modified version of $\mathcal{A}$ .22 2 One such example is $\mathcal{D}=\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\frac{1}{2})$ and $\mathcal{A}=\mathds{1}[\text{number of $1$'s in the sample is $0$ mod 100}]$ . As the sample size grows, an oblivious adversary can barely change the acceptance probability of $\mathcal{A}$ , whereas an adaptive one can change it completely.

Footnote 1 adds to the already-deep connections between the SQ framework and noise tolerance. The SQ framework was originally introduced in learning theory, where it continues to be influential in the design of learning algorithms that are resilient to random classification noise [Kea98]. Most relevant to the topic of this paper, to our knowledge across all noise models, all existing statistical algorithms that have been shown to be robust to adversarial noise can be cast in the SQ framework.

#### 1.1.3 Yes to Question 1 for additive noise

Our second result is an affirmative answer to Question 1 for one of the most natural types of corruptions:

#### Theorem 2.

The answer to Question 1 is “yes” for additive noise.

In additive noise, an oblivious adversary corrupts $\mathcal{D}$ to $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\mathcal{D}+\eta\mathcal{E}$ for an arbitrary distribution $\mathcal{E}$ of their choosing. An adaptive adversary, on the other hand, gets to inspect the sample $S$ drawn from $\mathcal{D}$ , and adds $\frac{\eta}{1-\eta}|S|$ many arbitrary points of their choosing to $S$ . The oblivious version of additive noise was introduced by Huber [Hub64] and has become known as Huber’s contamination model; the adaptive version is commonly called “data poisoning” in the security and machine learning literature.

Additive noise also captures the well-studied malicious noise (Definition 20) from learning theory [Val85] (see also [KL93]). Footnote 3 therefore shows that Huber’s contamination model, the malicious noise model, and the adaptive version of additive noise, are in fact all equivalent. Our proof of Footnote 3 is constructive: we give an explicit description of how $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ can be obtained from $\mathcal{A}$ , and $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ preserves the computational and sample efficiency of $\mathcal{A}$ up to polynomial factors.

#### 1.1.4 Yes to Question 1 in its fullest generality? An approach via subsampling

Our proof of Footnote 3 is actually an instantiation of a broader approach towards answering Question 1 affirmatively in its fullest generality: showing that the answer is “yes” for all (reasonable) types of allowable corruptions and all algorithms. We introduce the following definition:

#### Definition 1 (Neutralizing filter).

Let $\rho$ be a cost function and $\mathcal{A}$ be an algorithm for a statistical problem over a domain $\mathcal{X}$ . We say that a randomized function $\Phi:\mathcal{X}^{*}\to\mathcal{X}^{*}$ is a neutralizing filter for $\mathcal{A}$ with respect to $\rho$ if the following holds. For all distributions $\mathcal{D}$ , with high probability over the draw of $\bm{S}$ from $\mathcal{D}$ , the behavior of

$\mathcal{A}$ on $\Phi(\widehat{\bm{S}})$ , where $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ is a corruption of $\bm{S}$ by an adaptive $\rho$ -adversary,

well-approximates the behavior of

$\mathcal{A}$ on a sample from $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ , where $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ is a corruption of $\mathcal{D}$ by an oblivious $\rho$ -adversary.

Perhaps the most natural filter in this context is the subsampling filter. For an $n$ -sample algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ , we request for a larger sample of size $m\geq n$ , allow the adaptive adversary to corrupt it, and then run $\mathcal{A}$ on a size- $n$ subsample of the corrupted size- $m$ sample. We call this the “ $m\to n$ subsampling filter” and denote it as $\Phi_{m\to n}$ . The hope here is for the randomness of the subsampling step to neutralize the adaptivity of the adversary.

The efficiency of the subsampling filter is measured by the overhead in sample complexity that it incurs, i.e. how much larger $m$ is relative to $n$ . Subsampling from a sample that is roughly the size of the domain of course makes adaptive adversaries equivalent to oblivious ones, but this renders a sample-efficient algorithm inefficient. We are interested whether the subsampling filter can be effective while only incurring a mild overhead in sample complexity.

We propose the following conjecture as a general approach towards answering Question 1:

#### Conjecture 1.

For all reasonable cost functions $\rho$ and $n$ -sample algorithms $\mathcal{A}$ , the subsampling filter $\Phi_{m\to n}$ is a neutralizing filter for $\mathcal{A}$ with respect to $\rho$ with $m=\mathrm{poly}(n,\log(|\mathcal{X}|))$ .

We obtain Footnote 3 by proving Conjecture 1 in the case of $\rho$ being additive noise. While we have not been able to prove Conjecture 1 for all $\rho$ ’s and all algorithms, we can show the following:

#### Theorem 3 (If it is possible, subsampling neutralizes adaptivity).

Let $\rho$ be a cost function and $\mathcal{A}$ be an $n$ -sample algorithm. Suppose there is an $m$ -sample algorithm $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ whose behavior in the presence of adaptive $\rho$ -adversaries well-approximates that of $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of oblivious $\rho$ -adversaries. Then $\Phi_{M\to n}$ is a neutralizing filter for $\mathcal{A}$ with respect to $\rho$ with $M=O(m^{2})$ .

We note that in the context of Footnote 4, we do not require $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ to be computationally efficient: as long as $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ is sample efficient, then our resulting algorithm, the subsampling filter applied to $\mathcal{A}$ , inherits the computational efficiency of $\mathcal{A}$ .

Finally, we show that the bound on $m$ in Conjecture 1 cannot be further strengthened to be independent of $|\mathcal{X}|$ , the size of the domain:

#### Theorem 4 (Subsampling lower bound).

Let $\rho$ be the cost function for additive noise and $\eta$ be the corruption budget. There is an $n$ -sample algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ such that for $m\leq O_{\eta}(n\log(|\mathcal{X}|)/\log^{2}n)$ , $\Phi_{m\to n}$ is not a neutralizing filter for $\mathcal{A}$ with respect to $\rho$ .

While Footnote 5 shows that some dependence on $|\mathcal{X}|$ is necessary, we remark that the $\log(|\mathcal{X}|)$ dependence in Conjecture 1 is fairly mild—this is the description length of a sample point $x\in\mathcal{X}$ . Footnote 5 also shows that the quantiative bounds that we achieve for Footnote 3 has an optimal dependence on $|\mathcal{X}|$ .

### 1.2 Other related work

#### A separation result

Recently, Deng et al. gave a separation between the adaptive adversary, which they call “data-aware”, and the oblivious adversary [DGJ+21]. Specifically they showed that there are settings in which a natural Lasso-based algorithm for feature selection will often fail to select the correct features in the presence of an adaptive additive adversary, but would succeed in the presence of an oblivious additive adversary. Our Footnote 3 implies that this Lasso-based algorithm would succeed if it used the subsampling filter to preprocess its sample.

#### The online and dynamic setting

While the focus of our work is on the statistical setting, the distinction between adaptive and oblivious adversaries has also been the subject of recent study in the online [HRS21, ABED+21] and dynamic [BKM+22] setting, albeit with a notably different notion of adaptivity. In these settings, the adaptive adversaries can change the input distribution in response to the previous behavior of the algorithm, while oblivious adversaries must choose a fixed input distribution before the algorithms run.

#### Adaptive data analysis

We emphasize the distinction between the focus of our work and the recent fruitful line of work on adaptive data analysis ([DFH+15, HU14, SU15, BNS+21]). The focus of our work is on the adaptivity of the adversary, whereas the focus of this line of work is on the adaptivity of the SQ algorithm. Throughout this work, we reserve the use of “adaptive” to refer to the adversary, and all SQ algorithms will inherently be adaptive.

### 1.3 Discussion and future work

#### Implications of our results

Footnote 1 says that for all reasonable cost functions, all SQ algorithms (existing and future ones) that are resilient to oblivious adversaries are “automatically” also resilient to adaptive adversaries. Likewise, lower bounds against adaptive adversaries immediately yield lower bounds against oblivious ones. The same remark further applies for all algorithms in the case of additive noise and malicious noise, by Footnote 3.

As a concrete example, we recall that the agnostic learning framework was originally defined with respect to oblivious adversaries [Hau92, KSS94]. As in the PAC model there a concept class $\mathcal{C}$ , but the target function $f$ is no longer assumed to lie within $\mathcal{C}$ —hence the name of the model. The learning algorithm is expected to achieve error close to $\mathrm{opt}$ , the distance from $f$ to $\mathcal{C}$ . However, many papers on agnostic learning provide the viewpoint of an adaptive corruption process as intuition for the model: the data is assumed to be a labeled according to a function $f\in\mathcal{C}$ , but an adversary corrupts an $\mathrm{opt}$ fraction of the labels given to the learning algorithm. This adaptive version was subsequently defined as a separate model called nasty classification noise [BEK02] (as a special case of the nasty sample noise model introduced in that paper). Footnote 1 therefore shows that the agnostic learning model and the nasty classification noise model are in fact equivalent when it comes to SQ algorithms.

#### When can quantifiers be swapped?

The distinction between oblivious and adaptive adversaries can be viewed as a difference in the order of “for all” and “with high probability” quantifiers in the performance guarantees of statistical algorithms. An algorithm succeeds in the presence of oblivious adversaries if for all distributions $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ that are close to $\mathcal{D}$ , the algorithm succeeds with high probability over a sample $\bm{S}$ drawn from $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ . On the other hand, an algorithm succeeds in the presence of adaptive adversaries if with high probability over a sample $\bm{S}$ drawn from $\mathcal{D}$ , the algorithm succeeds for all corruptions $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ that are close to $\bm{S}$ . Our work formalizes the question of when these quantifiers can be swapped, and our results provide several answers.

#### Future work

In this work we initiate the systematic study of the power of adaptivity in statistical adversaries. A concrete direction for future work is to answer Question 1 for other broad classes of algorithms and natural noise models, either via the subsampling filter (Conjecture 1) or otherwise. Here we highlight the specific case of subtractive noise: having resolved the case of additive noise in this work, doing so for subtractive noise as well would be a significant step towards resolving Question 1 for all three generic noise models described in Section 3.

## 2 Preliminaries

We use boldface (e.g. $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ ) to denote random variables. Throughout this paper $\mathcal{X}$ denotes an arbitrary finite domain66 6 See Appendix B for remarks regarding infinite domains., and we write $S\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ to represent a multiset of elements in $\mathcal{X}$ , meaning $S\in\mathcal{X}^{0}\cup\mathcal{X}^{1}\cup\mathcal{X}^{2}\ldots$ . We use the notation $a=b\pm\varepsilon$ to indicate that $|a-b|<\varepsilon$ . For any $m\in\mathds{N}$ , the notation $[m]$ indicates the set $\{1,2,\ldots,m\}$ .

#### Distributions.

For any $S\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ , we use $\mathcal{U}(S)$ to refer to the uniform distribution over $S$ . For simplicity, we enforce that all distributions only have rational probabilities, meaning $\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}}[\bm{x}=x]$ is rational for any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and element $x\in\mathcal{X}$ .77 7 Alternatively, one could enforce that the cost function smoothly interpolate to irrational probabilities, which is the case for all standard noise models. For any distributions $\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2}$ and parameter $\theta\in[0,1]$ , we use $\theta\mathcal{D}_{1}+(1-\theta)\mathcal{D}_{2}$ to refer to the mixture distribution which samples from $\mathcal{D}_{1}$ with probability $\theta$ and from $\mathcal{D}_{2}$ with probability $(1-\theta)$

#### Definition 2 (Total variation distance).

Let $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ be any two distributions over the same domain, $\mathcal{X}$ . It is well known that the following are equivalent definitions for the total variation distance between $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ , denoted $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})$ :

- 1. It is characterized by the best test distinguishing the two distributions:

$$ \operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\coloneqq\sup_{T:\mathcal{X}\to[0,1]}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}}[T(\bm{x})]-\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}[T(\bm{x}^{\prime})]\right\}. $$

- 2. It is characterized by the coupling which makes the two random variables different with the smallest probability.

$$ \operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\coloneqq\inf_{(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime})\text{ a coupling of }\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime}}\left\{\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}[\bm{x}\neq\bm{x}^{\prime}]\right\}. $$

## 3 Adversarial noise models

To reason generally about various noise adversarial models, we represent the types of allowable corruptions by a budget $\eta$ and cost function $\rho$ , which maps each ordered pair of distributions to some non-negative cost (or infinity). The cost need not be symmetrical.

#### Definition 3 ( $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversary).

Given some cost function $\rho$ and budget $\eta$ , an algorithm operating in the oblivious adversary model will receive the following input: If the true data distribution is $\mathcal{D}$ , then the algorithm will receive iid samples from an adversarial chosen $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ satisfying $\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\leq\eta$ .

#### Definition 4 ( $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversary).

Given some cost function $\rho$ and budget $\eta$ , an $n$ -sample algorithm operating in adaptive adversary model will receive the following input: If the true data distribution is $\mathcal{D}$ , first a clean sample $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}$ is generated, and then the algorithm will get an adversarially chosen $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ satisfying $\rho(\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}))\leq\eta$ .

We remark that the adaptive adversary as defined in Definition 4 is slightly stronger than the definitions usually considered, in the sense that there is usually a bound on the size of $\widehat{S}$ the adversary is allowed to produce. For example, in the nasty noise model (Definition 7), the adversary is only allowed to change points in the sample, and so $|\widehat{S}|=|S|$ . All of our results apply regardless of the size of $\widehat{S}$ .

### 3.1 Standard noise models from the literature

In this subsection, we present three generic adversary models and show how they are special cases of our framework with an appropriate choice of cost function. Other standard models, and how they fit within our framework, are given in Appendix A.

#### Definition 5 (Additive noise).

Given a size- $n$ sample $S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}$ and a corruption budget $\eta$ , the adaptive additive noise adversary is allowed to add $\lfloor n\cdot\eta/(1-\eta)\rfloor$ points to $S$ arbitrarily.

The additive noise model is captured by the cost function:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}}(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\coloneqq\inf_{\eta\in\mathds{R}_{\geq 0}}\left\{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\mathcal{D}+\eta\mathcal{E}\right\}\quad\text{ for some distribution }\mathcal{E}. $$

The oblivious version of additive noise is the well-known Huber contamination model [Hub64].

#### Definition 6 (Subtractive noise).

Given a size- $n$ sample $S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}$ and a corruption budget $\eta$ , the adaptive subtractive noise adversary is allowed to remove $\lfloor\eta n\rfloor$ points from $S$ arbitrarily.

The subtractive noise adversary is captured by the cost function:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\coloneqq\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}}(\widehat{\mathcal{D}},\mathcal{D}). $$

#### Definition 7 (Nasty noise).

Given a size- $n$ sample $S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}$ and a corruption budget $\eta$ , the adaptive nasty noise adversary is allowed to change up to $\lfloor\eta n\rfloor$ of the points in $S$ arbitrarily.

This noise model is also known as strong contamination, and as nasty sample noise (or simply nasty noise) in the context of supervised learning [BEK02]. It is captured by the cost function $\rho=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}$ .

## 4 Proof of Footnote 1: The SQ framework neutralizes adaptive adversaries

In this section we formally state and prove Footnote 1—namely that the behaviour of a Statistical Query (SQ) algorithm in the presence of adaptive adversaries is equivalent to its behaviour in the presence of oblivious adversaries.

#### Basics of the SQ framework.

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be a distribution over some domain $\mathcal{X}$ . A statistical query is a pair $(\phi,\tau)$ where $\phi:\mathcal{X}\to[-1,1]$ is the query and $\tau>0$ is a tolerance parameter. These queries can be answered by a statistical query oracle $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ which, given an SQ $(\phi,\tau)$ , returns a value $v$ equal to $\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}}[\phi(\bm{x})]$ up to an additive error of $\tau$ i.e. $v\in\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}}[\phi(\bm{x})]\pm\tau$ .

Throughout this section, we will use some convenient shorthand. For any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and multiset $S\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ , we write

$$ \phi(\mathcal{D})\coloneqq\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}}[\phi(\bm{x})]\quad\quad\text{and}\quad\quad\phi(S)\coloneqq\phi(\mathcal{U}(S))=\frac{1}{|S|}\sum_{x\in S}\phi(x). $$

A $k$ -query statistical query algorithm, $\mathcal{A}$ , is an algorithm that makes a sequence of statistical queries to the oracle $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ one by one, using the result of the previous queries to decide which statistical query to make next.

#### Definition 8 ( $k$ -query SQ Algorithm).

A $k$ -query SQ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ is a sequence of $k$ SQs

$$ (\phi^{(1)},\tau^{(1)}),(\phi^{(2)}_{v_{1}},\tau^{(2)}),(\phi^{(3)}_{v_{1},v_{2}},\tau^{(3)}),\ldots,(\phi^{(k)}_{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1}},\tau^{(k)}) $$

to $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ , where $\mathcal{A}$ ’s choice of the $(i+1)$ -st SQ can depend on $v_{1},\ldots,v_{i}$ which are the answers of $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ to the previous $i$ SQs. For notational simplicity, we make the standard assumption that all the $\tau$ ’s are the same.

#### Using mechanisms to implement $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ .

The SQ framework is a stylized model that cleanly facilitates theoretical analyses; It allows the algorithm designer to abstract away an algorithm’s interaction with a random sample and instead assume $\phi(\mathcal{D})$ can be accessed up to $\pm\tau$ accuracy.

For an SQ algorithm to be useful, the $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ oracle must be implemented. This is done by a mechanism which uses a random sample $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}$ to simulate $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ with high probability. The interaction between a mechanism and SQ algorithm is depicted in Figure 1.

*Figure 1: The interaction between a mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ and SQ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ .*

#### Definition 9 ( $(\tau,\delta)$ -accurate mechanisms).

A mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ is $(\tau,\delta)$ -accurate for $k$ -query SQ algorithms, if for any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and SQ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ , with probability at least $(1-\delta)$ over the randomness of $\bm{S}$ and $\mathcal{M}$ ,

$$ v_{i}=\phi^{(i)}(\mathcal{D})\pm\tau\quad\text{for all }i=1,\ldots,k $$

where $v_{i}$ and $\phi^{(i)}$ are defined as in Figure 1.

In this work, we focus on the $\tau$ -rounding mechanism.

#### Definition 10 ( $\tau$ -rounding mechanism).

Given a sample $S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}$ and query $\phi$ , the $\tau$ -rounding mechanism, denoted $\mathcal{M}_{\tau}$ , returns the answer $v=\mathrm{round}(\phi(S),\tau)$ where $\mathrm{round}(x,\tau)$ refers to $x$ rounded to the nearest integer multiple of $\tau$ .

#### Fact 4.1 (The $\tau$ -rounding mechanism is accurate).

For any $k\in\mathds{N}$ and $\delta,\tau>0$ , the $\tau$ -rounding mechanism with a sample size of

$$ n=O\left(\frac{k\log(1/\tau)+\log(1/\delta)}{\tau^{2}}\right) $$

is $(\tau,\delta)$ accurate for $k$ -query SQ algorithms.

#### Proof.

For each query, the $\mathcal{M}_{\tau}$ can return one of only $O(1/\tau)$ possible values (after rounding). The $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ query is chosen as a function of $v_{1},\ldots,v_{i-1}$ , so there are at most $O(1/\tau)^{i-1}$ possible choices for the $i^{\mathrm{th}}$ query, and only $O(1/\tau)^{k}$ total unique queries $\mathcal{A}$ could choose. Using a Chernoff bound and union bound over all possible queries, the probability $\mathcal{A}$ asks a query, $\phi$ , where $|\phi(\bm{S})-\phi(\mathcal{D})|\geq\tau/2$ is at most

$$ \exp\left(-\Omega(\tau^{2}n)+O(k\log(1/\tau))\right) $$

For the $n$ given in Fact 4.1, that probability is at most $\delta$ . The desired result follows from triangle inequality and $|\mathrm{round}(\phi(\bm{S}),\tau)-\phi(\bm{S})|\leq\tau/2$ . ∎

The existence of accurate mechanisms (as in Fact 4.1) is the key to the SQ framework: SQ algorithms can assume that they have access to a $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ oracle, because for modest sample sizes and tiny failure probabilities, mechanisms are a $\textsc{Stat}_{\mathcal{D}}$ oracle.

### 4.1 The SQ framework in the presence of adversarial noise.

The SQ framework naturally extends to oblivious adversaries.

#### Definition 11 ( $k$ -query SQ Algorithm with an oblivious adversary).

Fix a cost function $\rho$ and budget $\eta$ . An $k$ -query SQ algorithm, $\mathcal{A}$ , in the presence of a $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversary is a sequence of $k$ SQs

$$ (\phi^{(1)},\tau),(\phi^{(2)}_{v_{1}},\tau),(\phi^{(3)}_{v_{1},v_{2}},\tau),\ldots,(\phi^{(k)}_{v_{1},\ldots,v_{k-1}},\tau) $$

each of which are answered according to $\textsc{Stat}_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}$ for some $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ satisfying $\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\leq\eta$ . This $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ is the same for all queries, but adversarially chosen. $\mathcal{A}$ ’s choice of the $(i+1)$ -st SQ can depend on $v_{1},\ldots,v_{i}$ which are the answers of $\textsc{Stat}_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}$ to the previous $i$ SQs.

Once again, to run an SQ algorithm, the $\textsc{Stat}_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}$ oracle is implemented by a mechanism. Given a sample $\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ , any mechanism satisfying Definition 9 will be able to simulate the $\textsc{Stat}_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}$ oracle.

In the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries, first a clean sample $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}$ is drawn, and then the adversary chooses an $\eta$ -corruption $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ that is passed to the mechanism, as shown in Figure 2.

*Figure 2: The interaction between a mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ and SQ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of an adaptive adversary.*

Our goal is to show that there are mechanisms that can simulate $\textsc{Stat}_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}$ for some $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ $\eta$ -close to $\mathcal{D}$ given just the corrupted sample $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ .

#### Definition 12 ( $(\tau,\delta)$ -accurate in the presence of adaptive noise).

Fix a cost function $\rho$ , budget $\eta$ . A mechanism $\mathcal{M}$ is said to be $(\tau,\delta)$ -accurate for $k$ -query SQ algorithms in the presence of adaptive noise, if for any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and SQ algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ , the following holds. With probability at least $1-\delta$ over the randomness of $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}$ ,

$$ v_{i}=\phi^{(i)}(\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\pm\tau\quad\text{for all }i=1,\ldots,k $$

for some $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ $\eta$ -close to $\mathcal{D}$ , where $v_{i}$ and $\phi^{(i)}$ are defined as in Figure 2. In particular, this holds regardless of how the adversary chooses $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ .

If $\mathcal{A}$ succeeds given $\textsc{Stat}_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}$ for every distribution $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ that is $\eta$ -close to $\mathcal{D}$ (i.e. $\mathcal{A}$ is resilient to oblivious adversaries), then, with high probability, $\mathcal{A}$ also succeeds in the presence of an adaptive adversary when using a mechanism satisfying Definition 12. We will show that the rounding mechanism meets Definition 12 whenever $\rho$ is “reasonable” in the sense of the following definition; this property is easily satisfied by all standard cost functions.

#### Definition 13 (Closed under mixtures).

We say that $\rho$ is closed under mixtures if for any distributions $\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{1},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{2}$ and $\theta\in(0,1)$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\rho(\theta\mathcal{D}_{1}+(1-\theta)\mathcal{D}_{2},\theta\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{1}+(1-\theta)\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{2})\leq\max(\rho(\mathcal{D}_{1},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{1}),\rho(\mathcal{D}_{2},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{2})). $$

Requiring that $\rho$ is closed under mixtures enforces that the adaptive and oblivious adversaries “match up” in the sense of making the same types of changes. This is formalized in the following fact, for which we provide a short proof in Appendix C.

#### Fact 4.2.

Let $\rho$ be closed under mixtures, $\mathcal{D}$ be a distribution over $\mathcal{X}$ , $\eta$ be a corruption budget, and $n\in\mathds{N}$ . Suppose that for all $S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}$ , there is a corresponding $\widehat{S}$ satisfying $\rho(\mathcal{U}(S),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{S}))\leq\eta$ . Let $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ be the distribution where $\bm{x}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ is generated by: 1) Drawing $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}$ and 2), drawing $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}})$ . Then, $\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\leq\eta$ .

Our quantitative bounds will depend on a parameter that is related to the types of corruption the adversaries can make. Suppose that the adaptive adversary is required to keep the size of the corrupted sample the same as the clean sample ( $|\widehat{S}|=|S|$ ). In this case, we require that if two samples $S_{1}$ and $S_{2}$ differ in only one point, then for any $\widehat{S}_{1}$ that is $\eta$ -close to $S_{1}$ , there is some $\widehat{S}_{2}$ that is $\eta$ -close to $S_{2}$ where $\widehat{S}_{1}$ and $\widehat{S}_{2}$ differ in only a small number of points. The following definition generalizes that notion to the case where the adversary can also change the number of points in the sample.

#### Definition 14 ( $\ell$ -local).

For any $\ell>0$ , a cost function $\rho$ with budget $\eta$ is $\ell$ -local if for any distributions $\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2}$ and $\eta$ -corruption $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{1}$ of $\mathcal{D}_{1}$ , there is some $\eta$ -corruption $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{2}$ of $\mathcal{D}_{2}$ satisfying $\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{1},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{2})\leq\ell\cdot\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2})$

All of the adversary models in Section 3 are $1$ -local with the exception of the $\eta$ -subtractive noise, which is $\frac{1}{1-\eta}$ -local. We encourage the reader to think of $\ell$ as a constant.

We are now ready to state the formal version of Footnote 1, which generalizes Fact 4.1 to the setting of adversarial noise.

#### Theorem 5 (Formal version of Footnote 1).

For any $\ell$ -local cost function, adversary budget $\eta$ , $\delta,\tau>0$ , and $k\in\mathds{N}$ , the $\tau$ -rounding mechanism with a sample size of

$$ n=O\left(\frac{\ell^{2}(k\log(1/\tau)+\log(1/\delta))}{\tau^{2}}\right) $$

is $(\tau,\delta)$ accurate for $k$ -query SQ algorithm in the presence of adaptive noise.

## 5 Proof of Footnote 4: If adaptivity can be neutralized, subsampling does it

Towards tackling Question 1 for all algorithms, we define the subsampling filter, a natural “wrapper algorithm” that operates only on samples and can be applied to any existing algorithm:

#### Definition 15 (Subsampling Filter).

Define the subsampling filter $\Phi_{m\to n}:\mathcal{X}^{m}\to\mathcal{X}^{n}$ that, given a set $S\in\mathcal{X}^{m}$ , subsamples $n$ elements $\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(S)^{n}$ and returns them. We will also write $\Phi_{*\to n}$ when the size of $S$ is variable.

Intuitively, by requesting a large number of points $m$ and randomly subsampling points for the original algorithm, the filter should able to neutralise some of the power of the adaptive adversary, since the adversary cannot know which subsample the algorithm will receive. In this section we will prove Footnote 4 which, informally speaking, states that if the noise model is such that adaptivity can be neutralised, then subsampling does it. In the next section, we carry out this proof strategy for the specific case of additive noise and establish Footnote 3.

### 5.1 Definitions and the formal statement of Footnote 4

We begin by formalizing what it means for the behavior of an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of an oblivious adversary to be equivalent to that of an algorithm $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ in the presence of an adaptive adversary. Roughly speaking, that corresponds to the range of acceptance probabilities $\mathcal{A}$ can have with all possible oblivious adversaries being close to the range of acceptance probabilities that $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ can have with all possible adaptive adversaries.

#### Definition 16.

Fix a cost function $\rho$ , budget $\eta\geq 0$ , and distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X}$ . For an algorithm $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{*}\to\{0,1\}$ , we define:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\coloneqq\sup_{\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\leq\eta}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]\right\}, \displaystyle\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\coloneqq\inf_{\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\leq\eta}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]\right\}, $$

the maximum and minimum acceptance probabilities of $\mathcal{A}$ given an obliviously corrupted $\mathcal{D}$ . We similarly define the adaptive versions:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},m)\coloneqq\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m}}\Bigg[\sup_{\rho(\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}))\leq\eta}\left\{\mathcal{A}(\widehat{\bm{S}})\right\}\Bigg], \displaystyle\mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},m)\coloneqq\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m}}\Bigg[\inf_{\rho(\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}))\leq\eta}\left\{\mathcal{A}(\widehat{\bm{S}})\right\}\Bigg]. $$

#### Definition 17 ( $\varepsilon$ -equivalent).

Fix a cost function $\rho$ and a budget $\eta\geq 0$ . Let $\mathcal{A},\mathcal{A}^{\prime}:\mathcal{X}^{*}\to\{0,1\}$ be two algorithms. We say that $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is $(n,m,\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries if the following holds for all distributions $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X}$ :

$$ \mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A}^{\prime},\mathcal{D},m)=\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\pm\varepsilon, $$

and likewise for $\mathrm{Min}$ instead of $\mathrm{Max}$ . If the algorithms $\mathcal{A}$ or $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ are randomized, then these expectations are also over the randomness of the algorithms.

We now state the formal version of Footnote 4:

#### Theorem 6 (Formal version of Footnote 4: If it is possible, subsampling does it).

Fix a cost function $\rho$ and budget $\eta\geq 0$ . Suppose that $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ are algorithms where $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is $(n,m,\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries.

Consider the subsampling algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n}$ which, given a sample $S\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ , subsamples $n$ elements $\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(S)^{n}$ and returns $\mathcal{A}(\bm{S}^{\prime})$ . For

$$ M\coloneqq O\left(\frac{m^{2}\log(1/\varepsilon)^{2}}{\varepsilon^{5}}\right), $$

we have that $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is $(n,M,9\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries.

#### Remark 2 (Search to decision reduction).

In both Footnotes 3 and 4, we focus on decision algorithms that output a single bit $\{0,1\}$ , rather than the more general setting of search algorithms that output an answer from some set $\mathcal{Y}$ . This is without loss of generality. Given a search algorithm $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{*}\to\mathcal{Y}$ , and any set of “good outputs” $Y\subseteq\mathcal{Y}$ , we could define an algorithm $\mathcal{B}\coloneqq\mathds{1}_{Y}\circ\mathcal{A}$ where $\mathcal{B}(S)=1$ iff $\mathcal{A}(S)\in Y$ . Then, we can directly apply Footnotes 3 and 4 to $\mathcal{B}$ . ### 5.2 Proof of Theorem 6

Our proof of Theorem 6 relies on the following simple lemma. Roughly speaking, it states that sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement are nearly indistinguishable when the population is a quadratic factor larger than the number of samples.

#### Lemma 5.1.

For any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and integers $m,M\in\mathds{N}$ , let $\Phi_{M\to m}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ be the distribution with the following generative process: first draw a size- $M$ sample $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}$ , and then subsample, with replacement, $m$ points from $\bm{S}$ . Then

$$ \operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}^{m},\Phi_{M\to m}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M})\leq\frac{\binom{m}{2}}{M}. $$

#### Proof.

We describe a coupling of $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m}$ and $\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\Phi_{M\to m}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ such that $\operatorname{{Pr}}[\bm{S}\neq\bm{S}^{\prime}]\leq\binom{m}{2}/M$ .

- 1. Initialize $S$ and $S^{\prime}$ to be empty sets, and $y_{1},\ldots,x_{M}$ to be unset variables.

- 2. Repeat $m$ times: (a) Draw $\bm{i}\sim[M]$ uniformly. (b) If $y_{\bm{i}}$ is unset, draw $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ and set $y_{\bm{i}}\leftarrow\bm{x}$ . Then, add $\bm{x}$ to both $\bm{S}$ and $\bm{S}^{\prime}$ . (c) Otherwise, add $y_{\bm{i}}$ to $\bm{S}^{\prime}$ and sample $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ to add to $\bm{S}$ .

It is straightforward to verify that the above generative process leads to the distribution of $\bm{S}$ and $\bm{S}^{\prime}$ being that of $\mathcal{D}^{m}$ and $\Phi_{M\to m}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ respectively. Furthermore, if $\bm{S}\neq\bm{S}^{\prime}$ , that means there is some index $i\in[M]$ that was sampled at least twice. If we fix $j_{1}\neq j_{2}\in[m]$ and some $i\in[M]$ , the probability $i$ is the index chosen at steps $j_{1}$ and $j_{2}$ is $1/M^{2}$ . Union bounding over the $M$ choices for $i$ and $\binom{m}{2}$ for $j_{1},j_{2}$ gives that

$$ \operatorname{{Pr}}[\bm{S}\neq\bm{S}^{\prime}]\leq\frac{\binom{m}{2}}{M}. $$

The desired result follows from the definition of total variation cost, Definition 2. ∎

Lemma 5.1 will be used in conjunction with the following fact:

#### Fact 5.2.

Suppose there exists a test which, given $c$ samples from a distribution $\mathcal{E}$ that is either $\mathcal{D}_{0}$ or $\mathcal{D}_{1}$ , returns $0$ if $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{D}_{0}$ with probability at least $\frac{3}{4}$ , and returns $1$ if $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{D}_{1}$ with probability at least $\frac{3}{4}$ . Then,

$$ \operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2})\geq\frac{1}{2c}. $$

Together, Lemma 5.1 and Fact 5.2 imply that for appropriately chosen $m$ and $M$ , there is no sample-efficient test distinguishing $\mathcal{D}^{m}$ from $\Phi_{M\to m}\circ\mathcal{D}_{M}$ with high probability. We will use this to prove Theorem 6 by contradiction. Using the assumption that $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ is equivalent to $\mathcal{A}$ , we will design a sample-efficient test that approximates $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ and $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}$ for $\mathcal{A}$ with respect to both $\mathcal{D}^{m}$ and $\Phi_{M\to m}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ . We then show that if $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\Phi_{*\to n}\circ\mathcal{A}$ is not equivalent to $\mathcal{A}$ , then these values will distinguish the two distributions.

The following lemma carries out the first part of this plan:

#### Lemma 5.3.

Let $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ be as in Theorem 6. There is an estimator $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ that uses

$$ m^{\prime}\coloneqq\frac{m\log(2/\varepsilon)}{2\varepsilon^{2}} $$

samples from a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and returns an estimate of $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)$ that is accurate to $\pm 2\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ , and likewise an estimator $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}$ for $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}$ . Formally, for all distributions $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X}$ ,

$$ \mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}}\Big[\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})=\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\pm 2\varepsilon\Big]\geq 1-\varepsilon, $$

and likewise for $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}$ and $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}$ .

#### Proof.

We will prove the lemma for $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ and $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ ; the proof for Min instead of Max is identical. $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ computes an estimate satisfying:

$$ \mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}}\Big[\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})=\mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A^{\prime}},\mathcal{D},m)\pm\varepsilon\Big]\leq\varepsilon. $$

This is sufficient to guarantee that $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ ’s estimate is within $\pm 2\varepsilon$ of $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)$ by our assumption that $\mathcal{A}$ is $(n,m,\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}^{\prime}$ . To provide such an estimate, $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})$ draws $\log(2/\varepsilon)/(2\varepsilon^{2})$ many size- $m$ samples $\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m}$ . For each, it computes:

$$ \sup_{\rho(\widehat{\bm{S}^{\prime}},\bm{S}^{\prime})\leq\eta}\big\{\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(\widehat{\bm{S}^{\prime}})\big\} $$

and returns the average of these supremums. By the Chernoff bound, this average satisfies Equation 3. ∎

#### Remark 3.

We are only concerned with the sample efficiency of these estimators, not their time efficiency or even whether they are computable. Indeed, as stated, an algorithm computing the estimators would need to loop or infinitely many $\widehat{\bm{S}^{\prime}}\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ to compute Equation 4. For us they are just an analytical tool used to prove Theorem 6, the conclusion of which gives an algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n}$ that inherits the time efficiency of $\mathcal{A}$ .

The next lemma notes that the $\mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ of $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n}$ can be expressed in terms of the $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}$ of $\mathcal{A}$ . Formally:

#### Lemma 5.4.

$\displaystyle\mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}},\mathcal{D},M)=\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big],$ and likewise for $\mathrm{Min}$ instead of $\mathrm{Max}$ .

#### Proof.

The lemma follows from this series of identities:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}},\mathcal{D},M) \displaystyle=\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\Bigg[\sup_{\rho(\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}))\leq\eta}\left\{\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\widehat{\bm{S}})\right\}\Bigg] \mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta} \displaystyle=\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\Bigg[\sup_{\rho(\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}))\leq\eta}\left\{(\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n})(\widehat{\bm{S}})\right\}\Bigg] \mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}} \displaystyle=\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\Bigg[\sup_{\rho(\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),\mathcal{E})\leq\eta}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{E}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S}^{\prime})]\right\}\Bigg] \Phi_{*\to n} \displaystyle=\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big], \mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta} $$

where the penultimate identity also uses our convention that distributions have rational weights, and therefore can expressed as the uniform distribution over a sufficiently large multiset of elements. ∎

The following lemma completes the proof of Theorem 6.

#### Lemma 5.5.

Let $m^{\prime}$ be as in Lemma 5.3 and define $M\coloneqq 14(m^{\prime})^{2}/\varepsilon$ . Then

$$ \mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big]=\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\pm 9\varepsilon, $$

and likewise for $\mathrm{Min}$ instead of $\mathrm{Max}$ .

#### Proof.

Our proof proceed by contradiction: assuming that $\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big]$ is more than $9\varepsilon$ far from $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)$ , we will prove that

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}},\Phi_{M\to m^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M})\geq\frac{\varepsilon}{14}. $$

From Lemma 5.1, we know that

$$ \operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}},\Phi_{M\to m^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M})<\frac{(m^{\prime})^{2}}{M}=\frac{\varepsilon}{14}, $$

which yields the desired contradiction. To establish Equation 5, we design an algorithm that given $\lceil\frac{6}{\varepsilon}\rceil\leq\frac{7}{\varepsilon}$ samples from either $\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}$ from $\Phi_{M\to m^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ is able to distinguish them with probability $\frac{3}{4}$ . Once we do, the desired result follows from Fact 5.2.

Let $\mu\coloneqq\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)$ . First, we define

$$ \displaystyle\delta\coloneqq\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[|\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)-\mu|>4\varepsilon\big] $$

and we bound

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big]\leq(1-\delta)\cdot(\mu+4\varepsilon)+\delta\cdot 1\leq\mu+4\varepsilon+\delta. $$

Similarly,

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big] \displaystyle\geq(1-\delta)\cdot(\mu-4\varepsilon)+\delta\cdot 0 \displaystyle\geq\mu-4\varepsilon-\delta. \mu-4\varepsilon\leq 1 $$

Hence by our assumption that

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big]-\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\right|>9\varepsilon, $$

we can conclude that $\delta>5\varepsilon$ .

Now let $\mathcal{E}$ be either $\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}$ or $\Phi_{M\to m^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ . Our test to determine which $\mathcal{E}$ is will do the following: draw $\lceil\frac{6}{\varepsilon}\rceil$ samples from $\mathcal{E}$ , $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{E}$ , and run $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})$ on each. If less than a $2\varepsilon$ fraction of the estimates returned by $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})$ differ from $\mu$ in more than $\pm 2\varepsilon$ , return that $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}$ . Otherwise, return that $\mathcal{E}=\Phi_{M\to m^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ . We will prove this test succeeds with probability at least $1-e^{-2}\geq\frac{3}{4}$ . We consider the two possible cases:

- 1. Case 1: $\mathcal{E}=\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}$ . In this case, given a sample from $\mathcal{E}$ , $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})$ returns an estimate that is within $\pm 2\varepsilon$ of $\mu$ with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ . By the Chernoff bound, given $\frac{6}{\varepsilon}$ such samples, the probability more than $2\varepsilon$ fraction deviate from $\mu$ by more than $\pm\varepsilon$ is at most $\exp(-\frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac{6}{\varepsilon}\cdot\varepsilon)=e^{-2}$ . Therefore, the test succeeds with probability at least $1-e^{-2}$ .

- 2. Case 2: $\mathcal{E}=\Phi_{M\to m^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ . We showed above that with probability at least $5\varepsilon$ over a sample $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}$ we have $\left|\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)-\mu\right|>4\varepsilon$ . When that’s the case, $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})$ returns an estimate that is further than $\pm 2\varepsilon$ from $\mu$ with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ . Therefore, on a single sample, the probability that the estimate of $\mathcal{A}$ deviates from $\mu$ by more than $\pm 2\varepsilon$ is at least $5\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)\geq 4\varepsilon$ . By the Chernoff bound, given $\frac{6}{\varepsilon}$ samples, the probability that at most $2\varepsilon$ fraction deviate $\mu$ by at most $\pm 2\varepsilon$ is at most $\exp(-\frac{1}{8}\cdot\frac{6}{\varepsilon}\cdot 4\varepsilon)=e^{-3}$ . Therefore, the test succeeds with probability at least $1-e^{-2}$ .

Hence, given $\lceil\frac{6}{\varepsilon}\rceil$ samples, it is possible to distinguish $\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}$ from $\Phi_{M\to m^{\prime}}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}$ with a success probability of at least $\frac{3}{4}$ . Equation 5 follows from Fact 5.2, completing the proof by contradiction. ∎

#### Remark 4 (Strong adaptive adversaries).

If $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ in the presence of oblivious adversaries is $(n,M,\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n}$ in the presence of adaptive adversaries, then it is also $(n,M,2\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ in the presence of strong adaptive adversaries (Definition 21 in Appendix B) as long as $M=\Omega(n^{2}/\varepsilon^{2})$ . This applies to both Theorem 6 in this section and Theorem 7 in the next.

Let $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ and $\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}$ be defined as in Definition 21. Then, for any strong adaptive adversary supplying the sample $\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}$ , there is some adaptive adversary supplying the sample $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ , so we wish to compare $\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}[\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime})]$ to $\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}[\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\widehat{\bm{S}})]$ . Recall that $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ first subsamples to $n$ points, so

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}[\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime})]-\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}[\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\widehat{\bm{S}})]\right| \displaystyle\leq n\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\widehat{\bm{S}},\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}}[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}))] \displaystyle\leq O(n/\sqrt{M})=\varepsilon. $$

## 6 Proof of Footnote 3: The subsampling filter neutralizes adaptive additive noise

In this section, we prove the following theorem:

#### Theorem 7 (Formal version of Footnote 3).

Fix a budget $\eta\geq 0$ , distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X}$ , and algorithm $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ . Consider the subsampling algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n}$ which, given a sample $S\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ , subsamples $n$ elements $\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(S)^{n}$ and returns $\mathcal{A}(\bm{S}^{\prime})$ . For

$$ M\coloneqq O\left(\frac{n^{4}\log(|\mathcal{X}|)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right), $$

we have that $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is $(n,M,\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ in the presence of $(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries.

Implicit in the proof of Theorem 6, we proved the following.

#### Lemma 6.1.

Fix a cost function $\rho$ , budget $\eta\geq 0$ , and $\varepsilon>0$ . Suppose that for an algorithm $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ , there are estimators $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta},\mathrm{Est\text{-}Min}_{\rho,\eta}:\mathcal{X}^{m}\to\{0,1\}$ that use $m$ samples from a distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and returns estimates satisfying

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m^{\prime}}}\Big[\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\bm{S})=\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\pm 2\varepsilon\Big]\geq 1-\varepsilon, $$

and likewise for $\mathrm{Min}$ instead of $\mathrm{Max}$ . Then, for

$$ \displaystyle M=\frac{14m^{2}}{\varepsilon}, $$

we have that $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is $(n,M,9\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries.

In order to prove Theorem 7, we’ll construct the estimator $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}$ (and likewise for Min). The goal is to estimate

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\coloneqq\sup_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\cdot\mathcal{D}+\eta\cdot\mathcal{E}}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]\right\}. $$

The key insight is rather than trying all possible distributions $\mathcal{E}$ , to compute a $\pm\varepsilon$ approximation, it suffices to consider those $\mathcal{E}$ that are equal to $\mathcal{U}(T)$ for some $T\in\mathcal{X}^{n^{2}/\varepsilon}$ . Our final result will have a logarithmic dependence on the number of $\mathcal{E}$ we need to try, which results in just a logarithmic dependence on $|\mathcal{X}|$ .

The following definition and accompany fact will be useful.

#### Definition 18 (Stochastic function).

For any sets $\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y}$ , a stochastic function ${\bm{f}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ is a collection of distributions $\{\mathcal{D}_{x}\mid x\in\mathcal{X}\}$ each supported on $\mathcal{Y}$ where the notation ${\bm{f}}(x)$ indicates an independent draw from $\mathcal{D}_{x}.$

#### Fact 6.2.

For any distribution $\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2}$ supported on a domain $\mathcal{X}$ , and any stochastic function ${\bm{f}}:\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{Y}$ , let ${\bm{f}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{i}$ be the distribution where to sample $\bm{y}\sim{\bm{f}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{i}$ , we first sample $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}_{i}$ and then sample $\bm{y}={\bm{f}}(\bm{x})$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}({\bm{f}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{1},{\bm{f}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{2})\leq\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}_{1},\mathcal{D}_{2}). $$

#### Proof.

Given a coupling of $\bm{x}_{1}\sim\mathcal{D}_{1}$ and $\bm{x}_{2}\sim\mathcal{D}_{2}$ , consider the coupling of $\bm{y}_{1}\sim{\bm{f}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{1}$ and $\bm{y}_{2}\sim{\bm{f}}\circ\mathcal{D}_{2}$ where if $\bm{x}_{1}=\bm{x}_{2}$ then $\bm{y}_{1}=\bm{y}_{2}={\bm{f}}(\bm{x}_{1})$ and otherwise $\bm{y}_{1}={\bm{f}}(\bm{x}_{1})$ and $\bm{y}_{2}={\bm{f}}(\bm{x}_{2})$ independently. Then,

$$ \operatorname{{Pr}}[\bm{y}_{1}\neq\bm{y}_{2}]\leq\operatorname{{Pr}}[\bm{x}_{1}\neq\bm{x}_{2}], $$

implying the desired result by Definition 2. ∎

To prove Theorem 7, we will design the estimators $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}$ and $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Min}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}$ . Plugging the sample complexity of those estimators into Lemma 6.1 would be sufficient for Theorem 7 with the slightly worse $M=n^{6}\log(|\mathcal{X}|)^{2}/\varepsilon^{7}$ . To get the optimal $\log(|\mathcal{X}|)$ dependence on the domain size (and an improved dependence on $n$ and $\varepsilon$ ), we need a more refined version of Lemma 6.1 that takes advantage of the structure of the particular estimators we derive. The following Lemma applies for any cost function $\rho$ , but we will then design $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying Equation 6 specifically for $\rho=\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}}$ in Lemma 6.4.

#### Lemma 6.3.

Fix a cost function $\rho$ , budget $\eta\geq 0$ , $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ , and algorithm $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ . Suppose there is a set of stochastic functions $\mathcal{F}$ each $\mathcal{X}\to\mathcal{X}$ , that satisfy, for any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))]\right\}=\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\pm\varepsilon, $$

and likewise for $\mathrm{Min}$ instead of $\mathrm{Max}$ , where ${\bm{f}}(S)$ is shorthand for applying ${\bm{f}}$ element wise and independently to $S$ . Then:

- 1. There are estimators $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}$ and $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Min}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}$ meeting the requirements of Lemma 6.1 for

$$ m^{\prime}=O\left(\frac{n\log(|\mathcal{F}|/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^{2}}\right). $$

In particular, this implies that for

$$ M=O\left(\frac{n^{2}\log(|\mathcal{F}|/\varepsilon)^{2}}{\varepsilon^{5}}\right), $$

we have that $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is $(n,M,9\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries.

- 2. More directly, for $\displaystyle M=O\left(\frac{n^{2}\log(|\mathcal{F}|/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\right)$ (7) we have that $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is $(n,M,5\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ in the presence of $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries.

#### Proof.

We first give $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}$ satisfying the first item. For $r\coloneqq O(\frac{\log(|\mathcal{F}|/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^{2}})$ , let

$$ \mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}=\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\Bigg\{\underbrace{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\mathrm{trial}\in[r]}\left[\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}\left[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))\right]\right]}_{\coloneqq\mathrm{Est}^{({\bm{f}})}}\Bigg\}. $$

We note that as long as the samples are reused across different ${\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}$ that $m^{\prime}=rn$ samples from $\mathcal{D}$ suffices to compute the above expression. By Hoeffding’s inequality, for any fixed ${\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}$ , with probability at least $1-\frac{\varepsilon}{T}$

$$ \mathrm{Est}^{({\bm{f}})}=\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))]\pm\varepsilon. $$

By union bound, with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ , the above holds for every ${\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}$ . If so, $\mathrm{Est\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}$ has the desired accuracy by Equation 6.

Next, we prove the $M$ from Equation 7 suffices. By Lemma 5.4, it suffices to prove that

$$ \mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\big[\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),n)\big]=\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\rho,\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\pm 5\varepsilon, $$

and likewise for $\mathrm{Min}$ instead of $\mathrm{Max}$ . Applying Equation 6 to both sides of the above equation, it is sufficient to prove that

$$ \mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\bigg[\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\bigg\{\underbrace{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}_{n}\sim\mathcal{U}(\bm{S})^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}_{n}))]}_{\coloneqq g^{({\bm{f}})}(\bm{S})}\bigg\}\bigg]=\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))]\right\}\pm 3\varepsilon. $$

Fix a single ${\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}$ . We’ll use McDiarmid’s inequality (Fact 4.6) to say that $g^{({\bm{f}})}(\bm{S})$ concentrates around its mean. Take any $S\in\mathcal{X}^{M}$ and suppose we change one point in it to create $S^{\prime}$ . Then $|g^{({\bm{f}})}(S)-g^{({\bm{f}})}(S^{\prime})|$ is at most the probability that the changed point appears in $\bm{S}_{n}$ , which is at most $\frac{n}{M}$ . Applying McDiarmid’s inequality,

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m}}\left[g^{({\bm{f}})}(\bm{S})=\mu^{({\bm{f}})}\pm\varepsilon\right] \displaystyle\geq 1-2\exp\left(-\frac{2\varepsilon^{2}}{(n/M)^{2}M}\right) \mu^{({\bm{f}})}\coloneqq\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\left[g^{({\bm{f}})}(\bm{S})\right] \displaystyle\geq 1-\frac{\varepsilon}{|\mathcal{F}|}. M=O\left(\frac{n^{2}\log(|\mathcal{F}|/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon}\right) $$

By union bound, with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ , for every ${\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}$ we have that $g^{({\bm{f}})}(\bm{S})=\mu^{({\bm{f}})}\pm\varepsilon$ allowing us to bound the left hand side of Equation 8,

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{M}}\left[\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{g^{({\bm{f}})}(\bm{S})\right\}\right] \displaystyle=\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mu^{({\bm{f}})}\right\}\pm\varepsilon\pm\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m}}\left[g^{({\bm{f}})}(\bm{S})\neq\mu^{({\bm{f}})}\pm\varepsilon\text{ for some ${\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}$}\right] \displaystyle=\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mu^{({\bm{f}})}\right\}\pm 2\varepsilon. $$

Lastly, we want to compare the above to the right hand side of Equation 8 to $\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\mu^{({\bm{f}})}$ . Fix any ${\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}$ . Using the notation of Lemma 5.1,

$$ \mu^{({\bm{f}})}=\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\Phi_{M\to n}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}}\left[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))\right]. $$

Therefore,

$$ \displaystyle\left|\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mu^{({\bm{f}})}\right\}-\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))]\right\}\right| \displaystyle\leq\max_{{\bm{f}}\in[\mathcal{F}]}\left|\mu^{({\bm{f}})}-\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))]\right| \displaystyle\leq\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D}^{n},\Phi_{M\to n}\circ\mathcal{D}^{M}) \displaystyle\leq\frac{\binom{n}{2}}{M}\leq\varepsilon. $$

Therefore, the left hand term of Equation 8 is within $\pm 2\varepsilon$ of $\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\mu^{({\bm{f}})}$ and the right hand term is within $\pm\varepsilon$ of $\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\mu^{({\bm{f}})}$ . Hence, Equation 8 holds, completing this proof. ∎

In order to use Lemma 6.3, we need to design $\mathcal{F}$ and prove that it satisfies Equation 6 when $\rho=\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}}$ . The below lemma completes the proof of Theorem 7.

#### Lemma 6.4.

Fix a budget $\eta\geq 0$ , $\varepsilon\in(0,1]$ , and algorithm $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ . Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the set of $|\mathcal{X}|^{n^{2}/\varepsilon}$ stochastic functions defined below.

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{F}\coloneqq\{{\bm{f}}^{(T)}\mid T\in\mathcal{X}^{n^{2}/\varepsilon}\}\quad\quad\text{where}\quad{\bm{f}}^{(T)}(x)\coloneqq\begin{cases}x&\text{with probability $1-\eta$}\\
\bm{y}\text{ where $\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{U}(T)$}&\text{with probability $\eta$.}\end{cases} $$

Then for any $\mathcal{D}$ over $\mathcal{X}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))]\right\} \displaystyle=\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\pm\varepsilon \displaystyle=\sup_{\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\cdot\mathcal{D}+\eta\cdot\mathcal{E}}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]\right\}\pm\varepsilon, $$

and likewise for $\mathrm{Min}$ instead of $\mathrm{Max}$ .

#### Proof.

Fix any distribution $\mathcal{D}$ . First, we note that the distribution of ${\bm{f}}^{(T)}(\bm{x})$ where $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ is simply that of $(1-\eta)\cdot\mathcal{D}+\eta\cdot\mathcal{U}(T)$ . Therefore, one direction of the desired result is easy:

$$ \displaystyle\max_{{\bm{f}}\in\mathcal{F}}\left\{\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}(\bm{S}))]\right\}\leq\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n). $$

The remainder of this proof is devoted to proving the left hand side of the above equation is at most $\varepsilon$ smaller than the right hand side. Fix any distribution $\mathcal{E}$ and consider $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\cdot\mathcal{D}+\eta\cdot\mathcal{E}$ . We’ll show that

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{{\bm{T}}\sim\mathcal{E}^{n^{2}/\varepsilon}}\left[\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}^{{\bm{T}}}(\bm{S}))]\right]\geq\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]-\varepsilon. $$

In particular, the above implies there is a single choice for $T$ that is within $\varepsilon$ of $\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]$ . As this holds for all corruptions $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ , it implies the desired result.

To sample from $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}$ where $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\cdot\mathcal{D}+\eta\cdot\mathcal{E}$ we can first draw $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{E}^{n}$ and then return $\bm{h}(\bm{S})$ , applied element wise, where:

$$ \displaystyle\bm{h}(x)\coloneqq\begin{cases}\text{$\bm{y}$ where $\bm{y}\sim\mathcal{D}$}&\text{with probability $1-\eta$}\\
\text{$x$}&\text{with probability $\eta$.}\end{cases} $$

Therefore, the distribution of ${\bm{f}}^{{\bm{T}}}(\bm{S})$ on the left hand side of Equation 9 is $\bm{h}\circ\Phi_{n^{2}/\varepsilon\to n}\circ\mathcal{E}^{n^{2}/\varepsilon}$ (using the notation of Lemma 5.1 and Fact 6.2). Finally, we prove Equation 9 (recalling that $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\cdot\mathcal{D}+\eta\cdot\mathcal{E}$ )

$$ \displaystyle\left|\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{{\bm{T}}\sim\mathcal{E}^{n^{2}/\varepsilon}}\left[\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}({\bm{f}}^{{\bm{T}}}(\bm{S}))]\right]-\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]\right| \displaystyle\leq\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\bm{h}\circ\Phi_{n^{2}/\varepsilon\to n}\circ\mathcal{E}^{n^{2}/\varepsilon},\bm{h}\circ\mathcal{E}^{n}) \displaystyle\leq\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\Phi_{n^{2}/\varepsilon\to n}\circ\mathcal{E}^{n^{2}/\varepsilon},\mathcal{E}^{n}) \displaystyle\leq\varepsilon. $$

∎

## 7 Proof of Footnote 5: Lower bounds against the subsampling filter

In this section, we show a lower bound on $m$ needed for the subsampling filter to work. Our lower bound holds in the setting of additive noise and therefore also shows that the dependence on $|\mathcal{X}|$ in Theorem 7 is optimal.

#### Theorem 8 (Formal version of Footnote 5).

For any sample size $n$ , domain $\mathcal{X}$ with $|\mathcal{X}|=2^{d}$ for an integer $d$ , adversary budget $\eta$ , and $\varepsilon>0$ , there exists an algorithm $\mathcal{A}:\mathcal{X}^{n}\to\{0,1\}$ and corresponding subsampled algorithm $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}\circ\Phi_{*\to n}$ for which $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is not $(n,m,1-\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ in the presence of $(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries for any $m=O_{\eta}(n\log|\mathcal{X}|/\log^{2}n)$ .

Without loss of generality, we can consider the domain to be the Boolean hypercube, $\mathcal{X}=\{\pm 1\}^{d}$ . Otherwise, we could map the domain to the hypercube. For an appropriate threshold $t$ , we’ll define

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{A}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n})=\begin{cases}1&\text{if for every $x_{i}$, there is an $x_{j}$ with $j\neq i$ s.t. $\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle\geq t$,}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Let $\mathcal{D}$ be uniform over $\mathcal{X}$ . For any $\varepsilon>0$ , $n$ , and $d$ , we’ll show that there is a choice of $t$ such that:

- 1. Lemma 7.1: $\mathrm{Oblivious\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},n)\leq{{\varepsilon/2}}$ , meaning, for any $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\mathcal{D}+\eta\mathcal{E}$ , it is the case that $\operatorname{{\mathds{E}}}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]\leq\varepsilon/2$ .

- 2. Lemma 7.2: $\mathrm{Adaptive\text{-}Max}_{\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta}(\mathcal{A},\mathcal{D},m)\geq 1-\frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ whenever $m=O_{\eta}(n\log|\mathcal{X}|/\log^{2}n)$ , meaning that for $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{m}$ , the adaptive adversary can choose $\lfloor m\cdot\eta/(1-\eta)\rfloor$ points ${\bm{T}}$ to add to the sample for which $\displaystyle\operatorname{{\mathds{E}}}[\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\widehat{\bm{S}})]\geq 1-\textstyle\frac{\varepsilon}{2}\quad\text{where }\widehat{\bm{S}}=\bm{S}\cup{\bm{T}}.$

Together, these prove that $\mathcal{A}$ in the presence of $(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta)$ -oblivious adversaries is not $(n,m,1-\varepsilon)$ -equivalent to $\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}$ in the presence of $(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{add}},\eta)$ -adaptive adversaries.

#### Lemma 7.1.

For any distribution $\mathcal{E}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}=(1-\eta)\mathcal{D}+\eta\mathcal{E}$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})]<\varepsilon/2. $$

First, we note that for any $x^{\prime}\in\mathcal{X}$ and a clean sample $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ , the probability that $\langle\bm{x},x^{\prime}\rangle\geq t$ is small: by Hoeffding’s inequality, $\operatorname{{Pr}}_{\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}}[\langle\bm{x},x^{\prime}\rangle\geq t]\leq\exp(-t^{2}/2d)$ . $$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})] \displaystyle\leq\eta^{n}+\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S})\mid\text{at least one clean point in $\bm{S}$}] \displaystyle=\eta^{n}+\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}\\
\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n-1}\end{subarray}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S}\cup\{\bm{x}\})] \displaystyle\leq\eta^{n}+\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}\\
\bm{S}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{n-1}\end{subarray}}[\text{$\exists\bm{x}^{\prime}\in\bm{S}$ with $\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime}\rangle\geq t$}] \displaystyle\leq\eta^{n}+(n-1)\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\begin{subarray}{c}\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}\\
\bm{x}^{\prime}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}\end{subarray}}[\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime}\rangle\geq t] S \displaystyle\leq\eta^{n}+n\exp\left({-\frac{t^{2}}{2d}}\right). \bm{x} $$

This will be vanishingly small for the particular choice of $t$ determined in Lemma 7.2. ∎

#### Lemma 7.2.

For any $m=O_{\eta}(nd/\log^{2}n)$ , there exists an adversarial strategy that, given $\bm{S}\in\mathcal{D}^{m}$ , chooses $\lfloor m\cdot\eta/(1-\eta)\rfloor$ points ${\bm{T}}$ to add to the sample for which

$$ \displaystyle\operatorname{{\mathds{E}}}[\mathcal{A}_{\mathrm{sub}}(\widehat{\bm{S}})]\geq 1-\varepsilon/2\quad\text{where }\widehat{\bm{S}}=\bm{S}\cup{\bm{T}} $$

#### Proof.

Let $C={{\lfloor m\cdot\eta/(1-\eta)\rfloor}}$ be the number of points the adversary can add and denote the sample $\bm{S}=\{\bm{x}^{(1)},\ldots\bm{x}^{(m)}\}$ . The adversary constructs ${\bm{T}}=\{\bm{y}^{(1)},\ldots,\bm{y}^{(C)}\}$ by setting each $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ to be the elementwise majority of $k$ chosen points from $\bm{S}$ (where $k$ will be determined later). The idea is that $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ is a cluster center that will form a correlated pair with every one of these $k$ points, with high probability.

More formally, for each $j=1,\ldots,C$ , define $\bm{S}^{(j)}=\{x^{(1+(j-1)k\pmod{|\bm{S}|})},\ldots,x^{(jk\pmod{|\bm{S}|})}\}$ to be the $j$ -th chunk of $k$ points from $\bm{S}$ , with the indices wrapping around to the start of $\bm{S}$ as necessary. We take $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ to be the elementwise majority99 9 We can assume $k$ is odd for simplicity. of the points in $\bm{S}^{(j)}$ :

$$ \bm{y}^{(j)}_{\ell}\coloneqq\underset{\bm{x}\in S^{(j)}}{\text{Maj}}\{\bm{x}_{\ell}\}\qquad\text{for $\ell=1,\ldots,d$.} $$

First, we note that for a given $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ , with high probability, any point in $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}^{(j)}$ will have a large dot product with $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{(j)}\sim\mathcal{D}^{k}}[\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}^{(j)}\rangle] \displaystyle=\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{(j)}\sim\mathcal{D}^{k}}\left[\bm{x}_{\ell}\bm{y}^{(j)}_{\ell}\right] \displaystyle={{\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\left({\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{(j)}\sim\mathcal{D}^{k}}\left[\bm{x}_{\ell}=\bm{y}^{(j)}_{\ell}\right]-\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{(j)}\sim\mathcal{D}^{k}}\left[\bm{x}_{\ell}\neq\bm{y}^{(j)}_{\ell}\right]}\right)}} \displaystyle={{\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\left({\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{u}\sim\text{Bin}(k-1,\frac{1}{2})}\left[\bm{u}\geq\frac{(k-1)}{2}\right]-\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{u}\sim\text{Bin}(k-1,\frac{1}{2})}\left[\bm{u}<\frac{(k-1)}{2}\right]}\right)}} \displaystyle={{d\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{u}\sim\text{Bin}(k-1,\frac{1}{2})}\left[\bm{u}=\frac{(k-1)}{2}\right]}} \displaystyle=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}{\frac{d}{\sqrt{k}}}(1\pm o(1)). $$
