$$ \displaystyle.\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{(j)}\sim\mathcal{D}^{k}}\left[\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}^{(j)}\rangle<t\right] \displaystyle=\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{(j)}\sim\mathcal{D}^{k}}\left[\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}^{(j)}\rangle<\frac{\mu}{2}\right] \displaystyle\leq\exp\left[-\Theta\left({\frac{\mu^{2}}{d}}\right)\right] \displaystyle=\exp\left[-\Theta\left({\frac{d}{k}}\right)\right]. $$

The subsampling filter $\Phi_{*\to n}$ takes a random subsample of size $n$ from $\widehat{\bm{S}}=\bm{S}\cup{\bm{T}}$ (with replacement). We want to show, with high probability over size $n$ subsamples $\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}})^{n}$ , that $\mathcal{A}(\bm{S}^{\prime})=1$ . For any point $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}$ , we say $\bm{y}^{(j)}\in{\bm{T}}$ is “good” for $\bm{x}$ if $\bm{x}$ was in the cluster used to compute $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ , meaning $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}^{(j)}$ . Similarly, for any $\bm{y}^{(j)}\in{\bm{T}}$ , we say that $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}$ is “good” for $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ is $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}^{(j)}$ . By construction, a given $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}$ participates in the computation of at least $\lfloor Ck/m\rfloor=\Theta_{{{\eta}}}(k)$ many cluster centers $\bm{y}^{(j)}$ ’s, and so for each $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}$ , there are $\Theta_{{{\eta}}}(k)$ good $\bm{y}\text{'s}\in T$ . Similarly, there are exactly $k$ good $\bm{x}\text{'s}\in S$ for each $\bm{y}\in T$ . As $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ has size $\Theta_{\eta}(m)$ , for any $\bm{x}\in\bm{S}^{\prime}$ , using $\bm{c}_{\bm{x}}$ to denote the number of good points for $\bm{x}$ that show up in $\bm{S}^{\prime}$ , we have that $\bm{c}_{\bm{x}}$ is distributed as $\text{Bin}(n,\Omega_{\eta}(k/m))$ . This gives:

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}})^{n}}[\mathcal{A}(\bm{S}^{\prime})=0] \displaystyle=\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}})^{n}}[\text{$\exists\bm{x}\in\bm{S}^{\prime}$ s.t. $\forall\bm{x}^{\prime}\in\bm{S}^{\prime},\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime}\rangle<t$}] \displaystyle\leq n\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{x},\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}})^{n}}[\text{$\forall\bm{x}^{\prime}\in\bm{S}^{\prime},\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime}\rangle<t$}] \displaystyle\leq n\left[\operatorname{{Pr}}[\bm{c}_{\bm{x}}=0]+\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{x},\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}})^{n}}[\text{$\forall\bm{x}^{\prime}\in\bm{S}^{\prime},\langle\bm{x},\bm{x}^{\prime}\rangle<t$}\mid\bm{c}_{\bm{x}}\geq 1]\right] \displaystyle\leq n\left[\operatorname{{Pr}}[\bm{c}_{\bm{x}}=0]+\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{x},\bm{S}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}})^{n}}[\text{$\langle\bm{x},\bm{y}_{\bm{x}}\rangle<t$]}\right] \displaystyle\leq n\left({1-\Theta_{\eta}\left({\frac{k}{m}}\right)}\right)^{n}+n\exp\left[-\Theta_{\eta}\left({\frac{d}{k}}\right)\right]. $$

∎

#### Setting of parameters.

To complete the proof of Theorem 8, we need to choose $m$ and $k$ so that, all the terms in Lemma 7.1 and Lemma 7.2 are vanishingly small. In particular, we need $n\left({1-\Theta_{\eta}\left({{k}/{m}}\right)}\right)^{n}\to 0$ and $n\exp\left({-\Theta_{\eta}\left({{d}/{k}}\right)}\right)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ . If $k=\Omega_{\eta}(m\log n/n)$ and $d=\Omega_{\eta}(k\log n)=\Omega_{\eta}(m\log^{2}n/n)$ with sufficiently large constant factors, we get the desired result. In other words, as long as $m\leq O_{\eta}(nd/\log^{2}n)$ , the adaptive adversary is stronger than the oblivious adversary.

## Appendix A Other standard noise models

Here, we list other standard noise models and show they fall under our framework.

#### Definition 19 (Nasty classification noise [BEK02]).

Let the domain be $\mathcal{X}=X\times Y$ . Given a size- $n$ sample $S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}$ and a corruption budget $\eta$ , the adaptive nasty classification noise adversary is allowed to choose $\lfloor\eta n\rfloor$ points and for each one, change it from $(x,y)$ to $(x,\widehat{y})$ for arbitrary $\widehat{y}\in Y$ .

This model is captured by the cost function:

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{agn}}(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})=\begin{cases}\infty&\text{if $\mathcal{D}$ and $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ do not have the same marginal distribution over $\mathcal{X}$}\\
\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

The $(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{agn}},\eta)$ -oblivious adversary corresponds exactly to the well-studied agnostic learning model [Hau92, KSS94]. Hence, Footnote 1 implies that nasty classification noise and the agnostic learning model are identical for SQ algorithms.

The final noise model that we discuss is defined with respect to an adversary that has intermediate adaptive power:

#### Definition 20 (Malicious noise [Val85]).

In the malicious noise model where the adversary has corruption budget $\eta$ , a sample is generated point-by-point. For each point, independently with probability $1-\eta$ , that point is $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ . Otherwise, the adversary is allowed to make that point an arbitrary $x\in\mathcal{X}$ with knowledge of the previous points sampled but not the future points.

#### On the relationship between malicious noise and additive noise.

The malicious noise adversary does not have full adaptivity, as when they decide what point to add, they only have knowledge of previous points sampled and not future ones. We now show how to encode the fully adaptive version of malicious noise, in which the adversary knows all points in the sample when deciding corruptions, in our framework.

We first augment the domain to $\mathcal{X}^{\prime}=\mathcal{X}\cup\{\varnothing\}$ where $\varnothing$ will be used to indicate the adversary can change this point arbitrarily. We then let $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ be the distribution satisfying, for each $x\in\mathcal{X}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{D}^{\prime}=(1-\eta)\mathcal{D}+\eta\mathcal{D}_{\varnothing} $$

where $\mathcal{D}_{\varnothing}$ is the distribution that always outputs $\varnothing$ . We define the cost function to be

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{mal}}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime})=\begin{cases}\infty&\text{if $\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime}}[\bm{x}=\varnothing]>0$}\\
\infty&\text{if $\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime}}[\bm{x}=x]<\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{x}\sim\widehat{\mathcal{D}}}[\bm{x}=x]$ for any $x\in\mathcal{X}$}\\
0&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

Note that in order for $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime}$ to be a valid corruption of $\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ (i.e. $\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{mal}}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime})\neq\infty$ ), all of the probability mass of $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime}$ must be over $\mathcal{X}$ , with none on $\varnothing$ . The above provides an encoding of an adaptive adversary that is at least as powerful as malicious noise. To further understand the corresponding oblivious adversary, we note that, after fixing $\eta$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{mal}}(\mathcal{D}^{\prime},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime})\neq\infty\quad\text{if and only if}\quad\widehat{\mathcal{D}}^{\prime}=(1-\eta)\mathcal{D}+\eta\mathcal{E}\quad\text{for some distribution $\mathcal{E}$}. $$

Hence, the oblivious adversary corresponding to malicious noise is the same as the oblivious adversary for additive noise. Footnote 3 implies that the adaptive and oblivious versions of additive noise, as well as malicious noise, are all equivalent.

## Appendix B Technical remarks

#### Fixed budget vs. variable budget.

Consider the nasty noise model (Definition 7), corresponding to $\rho=\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}$ in our framework. Given a size- $n$ clean sample $\bm{S}$ , the adaptive adversary can choose any $\eta$ -fraction of the points to change arbitrarily to create the corrupted sample $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ . Often an alternative definition is used where the adversary is allowed to arbitrarily change $m$ points in $\bm{S}$ , where $m$ can vary based on the specific sample $\bm{S}$ , as long as the marginal distribution of $m$ over samples $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}$ is $\mathrm{Bin}(n,\eta)$ . This definition is used by [DKK+19, ZJS19] to show that the adaptive adversary can simulate any oblivious adversary. Technically, for our definition of an adaptive adversary with fixed budget $\eta$ , this fact is not strictly true.1010 10 For example, suppose $\mathcal{X}=\{0,1\}$ , $\mathcal{D}$ is the identically $0$ distribution, and $\eta=0.1$ . If a size- $10$ sample is taken, under our adaptive definition, $\widehat{S}$ will never have more than a single $1$ . However, the oblivious adversary can choose $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ that returns $1$ with probability $0.1$ and as a result is a non-zero chance that two $1$ ’s appear in a size- $10$ sample. However, all our results are readily extendable to these slightly stronger adaptive adversaries with random-budgets.

We define an adversary model which encompasses those adversaries with variable budgets. First, the adversary will generate a corrupted data set $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ . Then, it is allowed to change some points in that set to create $\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}$ as long as, most of the time, $\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}$ and $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ are close.

#### Definition 21 (Strong $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversary).

Given a cost function $\rho$ and budget $\eta$ , an $n$ -sample algorithm operating in the strong $(\rho,\eta)$ -adaptive adversary model will receive as input the sample $\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}$ where

- 1. If the true data distribution is $\mathcal{D}$ , first a clean sample $\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}$ is generated.

- 2. The adversary chooses a $\widehat{\bm{S}}$ satisfying $\rho(\mathcal{U}(\bm{S}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}))\leq\eta$ .

- 3. The adversary chooses some $\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}$ where, over the randomness of the original sample and the adversaries decisions, the following holds. $\displaystyle\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\widehat{\bm{S}},\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}}\left[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}))\geq t\right]$ $\displaystyle\leq\exp(-O(nt^{2}))\quad\quad\text{for all $t\in(0,1)$}.$ (12)

All of our upper bounds on the strength of adaptive adversaries also apply to the strong adaptive adversary. See Remark 1 for changes in the proof needed for Footnote 1. For Footnotes 3 and 4, we can use an even weaker restriction on the adversary and only require that

$$ \displaystyle\mathop{{\mathds{E}}\/}_{\widehat{\bm{S}},\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}}\left[\operatorname{dist}_{\mathrm{TV}}(\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{\bm{S}}^{\prime}))\right] \displaystyle=O(1/\sqrt{n}) $$

in place of Equation 12. See Remark 4 for how Equation 13 can be used to make Footnotes 3 and 4 work with strong adaptive adversaries.

#### Finite vs infinite domains.

For our analyses, we assume that the domain, $\mathcal{X}$ , is finite. Our goal is to understand when an algorithm that succeeds in the presence of an oblivious adversary implies an algorithm that succeeds in the presence of an adaptive adversary. Any algorithm that succeeds in the presence of an oblivious adversary can only read finitely many bits of each data point, effectively discretizing the domain.

That said, Footnote 1 also applies to infinite domains. If the domain is infinite, a more general definition of closed under mixtures is required in place of the simpler Definition 13

#### Definition 22 (Closed under mixtures, infinite domain).

We say that $\rho$ is closed under mixtures if for any distributions $\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ , and coupling of $\bm{x}\sim\mathcal{D}$ , $\bm{x}^{\prime}\sim\mathcal{D}^{\prime}$ and a latent variable $\bm{z}$ (over any domain),

$$ \rho(\mathcal{D},\mathcal{D}^{\prime})\leq\sup_{\bm{z}}\left\{\rho((\bm{x}\mid\bm{z}),(\bm{x}^{\prime}\mid\bm{z}))\right\}. $$

When the domain is finite, Definitions 13 and 22 are equivalent. When it is infinite, Definition 22 is needed to prove Fact 4.2. The remainder of the proof of Footnote 1 is identical.

## Appendix C Proof of Fact 4.2

#### Proof.

By a standard inductive argument, Definition 13 implies that for any $m\in\mathds{N}$ , weights $\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{m}\geq 0$ summing to $1$ and distributions $\mathcal{D}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{D}_{m},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{1},\ldots,\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{m}$ , that

$$ \displaystyle\rho\left(\sum_{i\in[m]}\theta_{i}\mathcal{D}_{i},\sum_{i\in[m]}\theta_{i}\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{i}\right)\leq\max_{i\in[m]}\left\{\rho\left(\mathcal{D}_{i},\widehat{\mathcal{D}}_{i}\right)\right\}. $$

The distribution $\mathcal{D}$ and $\widehat{\mathcal{D}}$ can be written as the mixtures

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{D} \displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}}\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\bm{S}=S]\mathcal{U}(S), \displaystyle\widehat{\mathcal{D}} \displaystyle=\sum_{S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}}\mathop{{\operatorname{{Pr}}}\/}_{\bm{S}\sim\mathcal{D}^{n}}[\bm{S}=S]\mathcal{U}(\widehat{S}). $$

Since $\rho(\mathcal{U}(S),\mathcal{U}(\widehat{S}))\leq\eta$ for every $S\in\mathcal{X}^{n}$ , we can conclude $\rho(\mathcal{D},\widehat{\mathcal{D}})\leq\eta$ . ∎
